7.0.s.en: (2) Paul's love and forbearance toward the Corinthians

7.0.0.en: Because we enjoy God's fatherhood and His promises to care for us and work in us by His grace, we must respond to this love with repentance and confession, to cut off all bodily and spiritual desires. Then we look to the Day of Judgment, so we fear God and strive toward holiness, to partake of the Holy Mysteries, to do good and to grow in the virtues. Titus reassures Paul about the repentance of the Corinthians

7.1.s.en: (1) The news of the Corinthians comforts Paul

7.1.0.en: Receive us: as apostles and servants of Christ, and accordingly receive our teachings, that is, the commandments of God.

7.1.1.en: We have wronged no man: we were not hasty in judging anyone. Perhaps some false teachers accused him of haste in judging the sinner of Corinth who committed fornication with his father's wife, whom he cut off from the Church for a period. We have corrupted no man: we have not caused anyone to stumble by our teachings and led him away from the truth.

7.1.2.en: We have defrauded no man: we had no material purpose, nor did we exploit anyone's money and possessions, as the false teachers did.

7.1.3.en: St. Paul asks them to receive him so that they may receive his teachings, because he dealt with them well, in all love and without personal purpose, and caused no one to stumble.

7.2.0.en: He calls them to receive God's teachings from their mouths, because they have not wronged them or exploited them. In clearing himself the Apostle did not intend to condemn the Corinthians, but that no one should doubt him, so that they would receive his teachings, and he affirms the depth of his love for them by saying that they are in his heart, that is, that they are his children and a part of him, because they are all members of one body, which is the Church; he rejoices in their joy and grieves in their grief.

7.2.1.en: To die and live with you: if you suffer and endure afflictions that approach death, we grieve for you and almost die with you.

7.2.2.en: To live with you: when you rejoice and live with God, we also are enthusiastic and rejoice.

7.3.0.en: The Apostle shows that he did not intend to condemn them, in that he:

7.3.1.en: 1- Trusts in their love and their faith.

7.3.2.en: 2- Boasts of them, and therefore is not inclined to blame them.

7.3.3.en: 3- When Paul passed through afflictions and heard their good news, he was greatly comforted and rejoiced.

7.4.0.en: Paul explained the afflictions he passed through in Macedonia in Greece, and the afflictions are divided into two kinds:

7.4.1.en: 1- Quarrels and oppositions from the Jews and the Gentiles to his preaching of Christ.

7.4.2.en: 2- His anxiety about the faith of the believers in Macedonia and the surrounding countries because of the doubts and oppositions of the false teachers and the agitation of the wicked against the Church.

7.5.0.en: Paul declares God's tenderness toward His children who humble themselves before Him in prayers of lowliness, as Paul and those with him did, so God encouraged them with the news that Titus brought from Corinth, because Paul had sent him to them to reassure himself about them and to encourage them.

7.6.0.en: Paul rejoiced at seeing Titus, his beloved son. He was also comforted in his afflictions by the news Titus brought him from the Corinthians, which includes:

7.6.1.en: 1- Their earnest desire: toward Paul, with great love.

7.6.2.en: 2- Their mourning: that is, repentance with weeping over their sins.

7.6.3.en: 3- Their fervent mind: for life with God and for establishing Paul's authority as a responsible bishop.

7.6.4.en: Thus what Titus reported was the cause of Paul's comfort during his sufferings in Macedonia.

7.6.5.en: Offer good, encouraging words to everyone you meet, and you will lighten his pain and support him in his afflictions, and be confident that you will be the first to be comforted and to rejoice when you do this, as a reward from God.

7.7.s.en: (2) Paul's joy at the repentance of the Corinthians

7.7.0.en: Here Paul speaks of his rebuke of the Corinthians in his first epistle because of the fornicator, as mentioned in its fifth chapter. This grieved them and stirred their feelings to repentance, so Paul meant what he said, or what God revealed to him and he wrote in the epistle. He did not regret that he grieved them for a time, as he says, "but for a season," because this sorrow led to their salvation and their keeping away from sins. Although his feelings as a father were affected and he regretted that he had grieved them, out of tender human feelings, he held fast to the word of God and declared it to them, because the most important thing is that they repent, even if his heart as a father suffered because of their sorrow. This shows the tenderness of Paul's feelings and his fatherhood.

7.8.0.en: That ye might receive damage by us in nothing: you lose nothing because of our teaching, but rather gain repentance.

7.8.1.en: Joy filled Paul's heart, not because of the Corinthians' sorrow, but because their sorrow turned into repentance. This sorrow is "after a godly manner," to distinguish it from sorrow over the loss of some material things. Thus by their sorrow and repentance they lost nothing, but received God's forgiveness and blessing.

7.9.0.en: Paul makes clear the difference between holy sorrow, that is, sorrow over the act of sin, which produces repentance and trust in God's forgiveness in the Sacrament of repentance and confession, and an inclination to a new beginning, so that the person holds fast to repentance and does not regret this sorrow, because it is the way to life with God and to salvation. In contrast, we find that sorrow over the loss of material things reveals man's attachment to these desires, and this is sin, and the wages of sin is eternal death if a person persists in it.

7.10.0.en: Here Paul shows the results of the repentance of the Corinthians, for the sorrow of repentance moved them to:

7.10.1.en: Carefulness: spiritual striving in cutting off sin and clinging to God in prayers and fasts. Clearing of yourselves: they rejected the sin of the fornicator and rejected their own sins in order to forsake them and live for God. Indignation: distress over their sins that separate them from God.

7.10.2.en: Fear: of God, so that they live before Him in purity.

7.10.3.en: Vehement desire: for the pure life with God and for acquiring the various virtues.

7.10.4.en: Revenge: on the fornicator, by cutting him off until he repents, and the discipline of everyone who violates God's commandments so that the Church remains pure.

7.10.5.en: Thus by their repentance they declared their submission to God, so they received His forgiveness and became innocent. This is the great work of repentance.

7.11.0.en: He that had done the wrong: the young man who committed fornication with his father's wife.

7.11.1.en: He that suffered wrong: the father whose son committed fornication with his wife, for the father was still alive. Our care for you: our love for you, that you may live pure and God's wrath may not come upon you. Paul shows his concern that the Church of Corinth live in purity. What moved him in cutting off the fornicator was not a personal grievance against him or a special pity for the father, whose wife the young man committed fornication with, but what moved him was his love for righteousness and the purity in which God wants the Church to live.

7.12.0.en: Paul declares the rest of his heart because of the comfort of the Corinthians and the rest that resulted from their repentance, and the Apostle's comfort increased because of the joy of Titus, his son and friend whom he trusts, because he saw with his own eyes their repentance and their spiritual conduct, so he was at rest about their spiritual life and put Paul's mind at ease, and Paul rejoiced more because the whole Church of Corinth lived in true repentance.

7.13.0.en: Paul took care to teach the Corinthians the whole truth, and not as the false teachers cast doubt on Paul's teachings for them. Paul also boasted of the virtues of the Corinthians before Titus before sending him to them. When Titus went to them, he was assured of their repentance and good conduct and that their works matched Paul's praise of them.

7.14.0.en: Titus's love for the Corinthians increased after he visited them, because of their obedience to the word of God and their welcome and reverence toward him.

7.15.0.en: Paul sums up his feelings toward the Corinthians, which are joy in them because of his confidence in them, since their repentance and obedience have become clear and strong.

7.15.1.en: Accept the advice or rebuke of others, especially your father of confession and your spiritual guide, for this is your medicine that saves you from your sins.

7.15.2.en: Collecting gifts from Corinth for the needy in Jerusalem

8.0.s.en: (1) The generosity of the gifts of the Macedonians

8.0.0.en: The churches of Macedonia: in northern Greece, and among their most famous churches are Philippi and Thessalonica.

8.0.1.en: Paul wrote to the Corinthians in the first epistle, calling them to collect alms for the needs of the poor believers in Jerusalem. Now he encourages them to give by mentioning the churches of Macedonia and their concern in collecting donations for the needy in Jerusalem.

8.1.0.en: The gifts of the Macedonians were distinguished not by their abundance, but rather because they came from believers who suffered from material poverty but enjoyed abundant and great spiritual joy, so they gave out of their need beyond what was expected of them, because of their love for Christ and their concern for the needy in Jerusalem.

8.2.0.en: Here Paul declares two important facts about the gifts of the churches of Macedonia, namely:

8.2.1.en: 1- That they gave beyond their ability, for they are poor and needy, yet they gave out of their need.

8.2.2.en: 2- Of their own accord, and not by orders from Paul or insistence from him, contrary to what happened in Corinth, so they were distinguished by their delicate sensitivity to the needy.

8.3.0.en: Here Paul shows two new virtues in the gifts of the Macedonians:

8.3.1.en: 1- Their urging Paul to accept their gifts, for their love for the needy was strong, and their poverty did not prevent them from this.

8.3.2.en: 2- Their humility, for they begged him not to refuse their gifts, so that they might enjoy the fellowship of love with their brethren in the body of Christ, that is, the Church, counting their sharing in the ministry of giving as a grace they did not deserve.

8.4.0.en: The fifth virtue in the giving of the Macedonians is their readiness to give all they had, even themselves. This is after the example of what Christ did, for He was not content with healing the sick and feeding the multitudes, but gave Himself on the cross for our salvation.

8.5.0.en: As the believers in Macedonia were moved to give to the needy in Jerusalem, Paul thought it good that the Corinthians share in this grace, that is, the ministry of giving. Titus had spoken to them about it when he was with them, and then visited them afterward and collected these gifts.

8.5.1.en: Any gift you give to the needy, whether materially, or in the soul by helping a poor person, visiting a sick person or caring for a person who suffers from psychological troubles, is a grace to you because you offer it to Christ, who rejoices greatly in your giving and rewards you with many blessings on earth and in heaven.

8.6.0.en: Paul praises the Corinthians for their concern to grow in the virtues, and he gave examples of them: Faith: in Christ and His work in them.

8.6.1.en: Utterance: speaking about spiritual matters and supporting and encouraging others.

8.6.2.en: Knowledge: the knowledge of God and the Church and everything in it.

8.6.3.en: Diligence: in repentance and rejecting sins, and also in acquiring the virtues.

8.6.4.en: Your love to us: in obeying Paul and esteeming his words and teachings.

8.6.5.en: Then he gently asks them to take care to grow in this grace, that is, the virtue of giving.

8.7.0.en: The Apostle shows that giving comes from love and sensitivity to others, and not merely obeying orders issued by Paul. He explained that he directs their attention to the concern of the Macedonians for giving, and then expects, as a result of their love and sincerity, that they also will give as much as they are able.

8.8.0.en: The Apostle offers a second encouragement to the Corinthians to give, after encouraging them with the giving of the Macedonians, and it is the greatest encouragement, because it is Christ Himself, who gave up everything by His Incarnation and was born in the humblest place, the manger, and lived in poverty in order to redeem us and satisfy us and enrich us by His gift to us. For He took what is ours and gave us what is His, as we say in the Friday Praise, so that we became partakers of the divine nature and heirs of the Kingdom. This is thus a motive for us to give up our comfort and care for and give to the needy. Christ gave up everything, while we give up a little of material things to give even the bare necessities to the needy. The devil prevails against them and makes them fall into sin, or shows their physical weakness before the wicked, but God strengthens them and heals them and raises them up again with power, so that they continue their striving and their ministry.

8.9.0.en: In this matter: collecting gifts for the needy in Jerusalem.

8.9.1.en: For this: the opinion and guidance that Paul gives about collecting the gifts.

8.9.2.en: Paul commends the Corinthians that they thought of collecting gifts for their needy brethren in Judea, and when the Macedonians heard of this they were moved and collected gifts. So Paul encourages the Corinthians to carry out what they thought of, as the Macedonians collected. And he gives them guidance in collecting the gifts, which he mentions in the following verses.

8.10.1.en: Out of that which ye have: according to your ability.

8.10.2.en: The Apostle encourages the Corinthians to complete their intention to donate to the needy. They should not be content with their desire and willingness to give, but complete this with diligence, that is, an actual collection of the gifts, according to each one's ability and his financial and spiritual capacity.

8.11.1.en: The Apostle confirms what was said in the previous verse, that the collection is to be according to each one's ability. So let no one demand of himself more than his ability, for God values the gift according to the love and self-sacrifice of the giver and not the quantity of the gift.

8.12.0.en: The Apostle completes the idea mentioned in the two preceding verses, which is that he does not mean that they should give up and give beyond their ability, so that they become poor and in distress for the ease of others. That is a high spiritual level, but it is enough that they give up a little so that others may have some relief like them.

8.13.0.en: Your abundance a supply for their want: the material gifts of the Corinthians that meet the needs of the needy in Jerusalem.

8.13.1.en: Their abundance also may be a supply for your want: the Apostles and servants whom the Church of Jerusalem sent to preach to the Gentiles, who meet their spiritual needs and fill them with Christ like the believers in Jerusalem.

8.13.2.en: Here the Apostle declares a truth, which is that when the churches of the Gentiles give to the needy in Judea, they at the same time receive spiritual gifts, that is, the preaching of Christ and the ministry and pastoral care that flow from Jerusalem. Each party gives some of what it has, the first giving material things and the second giving spiritual things, but not at anyone's expense or beyond anyone's ability. Whoever gives material or spiritual things gives some of what he has and not all that he has. Thus there is equality, that is, both parties are satisfied spiritually and materially as a result of the other's giving.

8.14.0.en: Paul confirms his words about equality among all by what happened with the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai when the manna fell on the ground around their tents and they went out to gather it every morning (Ex 16:18). The strong, who gathered much, took only what he needed and gave the rest to the weak, and the physically weak, who gathered little, took from the strong, so that everyone came out with a certain measure, which was a measure among the children of Israel called the omer, so everyone was satisfied and no one kept any of the manna until the next day, because it spoiled if it was kept overnight.

8.14.1.en: As Paul was gentle and encouraging to the Corinthians in giving, may you, when you ask someone for something, or direct him to correct some mistake, begin your words with praise and then encourage him gently, so that you win his love and reach what you want.

8.15.s.en: (3) Paul's testimony about those sent to collect the gifts

8.15.0.en: Care: concern for collecting the gifts.

8.15.2.en: Paul thanks God, who put the concern for collecting the gifts into the heart of Titus as into the heart of Paul, to collect them from the Corinthians, for God is the One who moves all virtues in us.

8.16.0.en: The exhortation: Paul asked Titus to go to Corinth to collect the donations.

8.16.1.en: Of his own accord: he was intending to go to Corinth, so he responded at once to Paul's request to him to do so.

8.16.2.en: Paul shows Titus's concern and diligence in collecting the gifts, so that he accepted to go to Corinth as soon as Paul asked him to.

8.17.0.en: In the gospel: that is, in the preaching.

8.17.1.en: Paul sent with Titus one of the servants who assisted him to help in collecting the gifts, and describes this servant as known and praised in all the churches of Macedonia in which he preached. He did not specify the identity of this servant, but he was most likely Luke, who accompanied Paul on most of his journeys, as the Book of Acts testifies.

8.18.0.en: This grace which is administered by us: collecting the donations that Paul commanded, in the collection of which his two assistants Titus and Luke shared.

8.18.1.en: The glory of the same Lord: Christ, in whom we all believe and whom we all worship, for these gifts glorify Him because they declare the love of His children for one another.

8.18.2.en: Your readiness of mind: your concern and love in offering the gifts.

8.18.3.en: Paul affirms and continues his praise of Luke, who was chosen to perform this ministry, that is, collecting the gifts, so that God may be glorified and their love for their brethren shown. Paul offers all this praise so that the Corinthians may trust Luke and give him their money.

8.19.0.en: Abundance: the greatness and largeness of the sum collected.

8.19.1.en: Administered: the ministry of collecting the gifts.

8.19.2.en: We see Paul's exactness in his caution in collecting the gifts, because the sum collected was large, so that no one would doubt him or one of his companions, which would lead them to doubt the teachings of Christ that he proclaims; he was careful to send trustworthy people to collect the gifts.

8.20.0.en: Paul did not collect the gifts himself and give them to the needy in Jerusalem, so that no one would suspect him. So he arranged for delegates on his behalf to collect the donations, as well as delegates from the people of the countries, so that all the people would be assured that their gifts were in faithful hands, and thus no one would stumble.

8.21.0.en: Paul sent with Titus and Luke a third servant who was distinguished by his concern and diligence in the ministry, and was even enthusiastic about the ministry of collecting gifts from the Corinthians because of his confidence in their love and self-giving, so he came forward to Paul wishing to share in this ministry. He was one of Paul's companions to Jerusalem and was most likely Tychicus (Acts 20:4).

8.22.0.en: Paul sums up his recommendation and testimony about those sent to collect the gifts from the Corinthians. They are Titus, whom he describes as his partner in the ministry and preaching, and the two brethren accompanying Titus, who are most likely Luke and Tychicus, whom he describes as messengers of the churches of the Gentiles and delegates for them in collecting the donations and delivering them to Jerusalem to declare the glory of Christ in the love of the believers for one another.

8.23.0.en: Shew ye to them: show your love to these three delegates in the generosity of your giving. Before the churches: considering these messengers as delegates of the churches of Macedonia, which had gone ahead and collected for the needy, so show them your love also in your gifts.

8.23.1.en: The proof of your love: the evidence of your love.

8.23.2.en: Of our boasting on your behalf: considering that Paul is their apostle and they are his children, their love and their giving gladden him and he boasts of it.

8.23.3.en: Finally Paul encourages them to be generous in giving for the sake of God and His three servants who will collect the donations, and so that he also may rejoice and boast in their love.

8.23.4.en: It is good that your heart be pure before God, but care also for people's feelings, so do not cause anyone to stumble, even unintentionally. And care to draw everyone by your love for Christ, and let us not forget to provide for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (v. 21). Attention to generous giving with cheerfulness
